cells.tense: The work is done and sitting there, and your read on it has settled too.
cells.act: let several things be true and act on one
cells.ask: Name everything that's true about a piece of work you're finishing this week, without sorting it down to one reading. Act on one of them by Friday. The others can stay where they are.
cells.core:
Something is close to done, and you can say where it stands without overselling it. The claim you make about it stays small. That isn't modesty. It's what keeps the last step steady while the last step gets taken.

More than one reading of the thing is true, and you don't have to narrow it to one to set it down. Put them all on paper, mark the one you'll act on now, and leave the other marks alone. A finished thing doesn't get finished by being explained, and it doesn't need a single account of itself to leave your hands. What goes out goes out whole, and the marks you didn't pick weren't the loose ends.
cells.sheetLine: You can finish something without deciding what it means.
cells.verb: assert the frame outward until it holds
cells.place: the moment something is finished and can be let go of

cells.tense: The frame is already up over a space the thing itself hasn't filled yet.
cells.act: go all the way into the pattern until you meet its edge
cells.ask: Take a claim you've made about how a project should work and follow it to the point where it stops holding. Not at the first snag. To the edge of it, and stop there.
cells.core:
You can build a frame around something before the thing itself has arrived, and the frame is honestly good. Solid, well-argued, ready for occupants. You can also keep going after you've hit the spot where the frame stops covering the thing, laying proof over the gap so nobody sees it. That's the part that costs. People working near you start doing the careful version of their part so the frame doesn't move.

Go into the argument all the way. Pick a claim you've made about how this should work and follow it to where it stops holding, then stop. Don't shore it up. The edge is information you can't get by defending the middle. You'll likely come back with the same frame and one honest doorway in it, and the people nearby can finally walk through.
cells.sheetLine: You can defend a frame past the point it fits.
cells.verb: assert the frame outward until it holds

cells.tense: A piece of work is close enough to done that finishing it keeps sliding to tomorrow.
cells.act: return to the work daily until it is profound
cells.ask: Pick the smallest unfinished piece of it and put one short stretch into it on most days this week. Ten minutes counts. Stop when the stretch is up instead of chasing the whole thing.
cells.core:
There's something near enough to finished that finishing keeps being tomorrow's item, and it has been tomorrow's item for a while. Not because you can't do it. Because the frame you'd have to put around the thing to call it declared and done and out in the world is one nobody is asking you for, and the gap between almost and finished is where you've been standing with the lights off.

The way through isn't a decision. It's minutes. Take the smallest unfinished piece and put a short stretch into it on most days this week, ten minutes if that's what there is. Stop when each stretch is up instead of trying to close the whole thing in one push. Showing up for a week gets you further than any plan for it, and the work itself hands you the rest.
cells.sheetLine: The last unfinished thing has been tomorrow's for a while.
cells.verb: assert the frame outward until it holds
cells.place: the moment something is finished and can be let go of

cells.tense: You've been weighing the quality of what happens near you for a long time without calling it weighing.
cells.act: count what the ending gave you
cells.ask: Take something that finished near you recently, small or large. Set down three things it left behind that are still here. On paper, not in your head. Nothing about what should have gone differently.
cells.core:
People bring you the thing they've made and leave steadier, and the calm gets credited to the thing itself. Their plan was good, they'll say, when what happened was that you looked at it and called it solid, and they believed you. You'd tell it the other way. You were just around. The ones who bring you things have noticed what you actually do, and they keep coming back for it.

Claim it by counting what it made. Take a piece of work that ended near you — a project, a season, a stretch of something — and set down three things it left behind that are still here. Tangible ones. Nothing about how it should have gone. Watch how the list reads in your own handwriting. That's the yield, and it came through you, and there's no version of the story where it didn't.
cells.sheetLine: The quality showing in what people bring you is yours.
cells.verb: assert the frame outward until it holds
cells.place: the moment something is finished and can be let go of

attempts.check: The record supports that Assertion imposes structure through Intent, and the seat names the moment of completion; it does not support naming what the person 'really' wants or what they fear. A reader might fairly say they have never once had the urge to declare or organize, that they finish quietly and that is enough; the asks are written as one bounded move a camera could see, so they survive that objection. The sentence that serves me more than the person is any clause implying the shape of what they will build — everything here stays on the habit of finishing, not its content.
